Reject invalid HPACK index 0 before invoking the header handler.

## Description

RFC 7541 section 6.1 requires index 0 in an indexed header field to be treated as a decoding error. The decoder previously forwarded it to the header handler, where the static-table lookup threw IndexOutOfRangeException. Reject it with HPackDecodingException and the existing invalid-index message instead.

Adds a zero-index regression test and valid HPACK static-table boundary coverage. Also adds QPACK boundary tests for indexed fields and name references: unlike HPACK, QPACK uses zero-based indexes, so index 0 remains valid. HPACK literal-name marker 0 is unchanged.

Issues.Title: Unquarantine BlazorWasmTemplateTest
Issues.Body:
Fix offline PWA menu validation and unquarantine BlazorWasmTemplateTest.

## Description

Remove the `QuarantinedTest` attribute associated with #66293 so all methods in `BlazorWasmTemplateTest` return to normal CI, and fix the shared navigation helper's incorrect assumption that the menu always starts collapsed. No product or template content is changed.

The original NU1603 DevServer version-pin defect was fixed in #66303. Across all 68 completed `aspnetcore-quarantined-pr` builds on `main` during October 19–26, 2026, the standalone and Azure Active Directory methods passed, while the PWA method failed with a different error, not NU1603.

The PWA test was timing out waiting for `.nav-scrollable` to become visible during its offline interaction check. This failure was caused by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/68768 applied on disabled tests.

The standalone template toggles its menu state when a navigation link is clicked, including at desktop width where CSS keeps it visible. The online interaction check visits Counter and Weather, toggling twice. The offline check excludes Weather and visits only Counter, leaving the menu expanded. After narrowing the viewport, the helper's unconditional toggler click closes that already-open menu, and its wait for a visible menu times out.

`VerifyNavMenuCollapsesAfterNavigationAsync` now clicks the toggler only when `.nav-scrollable` is hidden. The existing visibility wait, Home navigation, collapse assertion, and viewport restoration remain unchanged. The existing PWA test already exercises the regression-producing sequence.

Fixes #66293

- **Head:** `pureween-pr-review-behavioral-evals` at `229c191bb51a39d071014eadc8a039cb9a744cc4`

Positive missing/error controls and negatives for partial/late manifest, worker dispatch, later success, non-BLOCKED output, and fixture tampering all pass. |
| Producer/checker and grader responsibilities stay separate | The inherited C# suite proves producer/checker behavior; 20 fixture controls prove committed synthetic fixture fidelity; 64 trajectory controls prove grader discrimination. Synthetic controls do not claim live subject compliance. |

Independent GPT-5.6 and Gemini reviews were run after deterministic validation. Their concrete findings were rubber-ducked before edits and addressed, including complete-manifest ordering, standard fixture-test integration, worker dispatch inputs/configuration, strongest-candidate and synthesis ordering, candidate-fixture fail-closed behavior, and worker `rg` role scopes. Issues.Title: Identity API /manage/2fa ignores IdentityResult from SetTwoFactorEnabledAsync
Issues.Body:
## Summary

The Identity API `POST /manage/2fa` endpoint ignores the `IdentityResult` returned by `UserManager.SetTwoFactorEnabledAsync`. When that update fails (for example with an optimistic concurrency failure), the endpoint continues as though the change was applied and returns a success response.

## What is wrong

* `SetTwoFactorEnabledAsync` returns an `IdentityResult` that reports store update failures (such as `ConcurrencyFailure`) rather than throwing. The endpoint awaits it and discards the result.
* The response therefore does not reliably reflect whether two-factor authentication was actually enabled or disabled. Subsequent steps (shared key reset, recovery code generation) also run against a state that may not have been persisted.
* Every other mutating endpoint in the same file checks `result.Succeeded` and returns `CreateValidationProblem(result)`; this endpoint is inconsistent with that pattern.
* Concurrent updates to the same user record (for example, other operations that update the user row such as failed sign-in bookkeeping) can make the update fail with a concurrency result, so this is reachable in normal operation.

## Why it matters (defense in depth)

* Correctness: callers cannot distinguish a persisted change from a rejected one, and a security-relevant setting (2FA enabled/disabled) can end up different from what the client was told.
* Hardening: security-sensitive state transitions should be fail-closed and report failure to the caller so clients can retry or surface an error.

## Affected code

* src/Identity/Core/src/IdentityApiEndpointRouteBuilderExtensions.cs:532 - `SetTwoFactorEnabledAsync(user, true)` result ignored
* src/Identity/Core/src/IdentityApiEndpointRouteBuilderExtensions.cs:536 - `SetTwoFactorEnabledAsync(user, false)` result ignored
* src/Identity/Core/src/IdentityApiEndpointRouteBuilderExtensions.cs:539-542 - `ResetAuthenticatorKeyAsync` result in the same handler is also ignored (same class of issue; also again in the "no key yet" branch of the handler)

## Recommended fix

* Selected approach: capture the `IdentityResult` from both `SetTwoFactorEnabledAsync` calls and, when `!Succeeded`, return `CreateValidationProblem(result)`, matching the pattern already used by the passkey, password, and email endpoints. The handler's return type already includes `ValidationProblem`, so there is no public API or response-shape change for existing success paths.
* Alternatives considered:
  * Throwing on failure: rejected; it would surface as a 500 and diverges from the rest of the endpoints.
  * Retrying on concurrency failure inside the endpoint: rejected as larger behavior change; clients can retry on the validation problem.
* Follow-up consideration: apply the same check to `ResetAuthenticatorKeyAsync` calls in the handler; `GenerateNewTwoFactorRecoveryCodesAsync` returns a nullable enumerable instead of an `IdentityResult`, so its failure signal (`null`) needs a separate decision.
* Compatibility: previously silent failures now return HTTP 400 with an `application/problem+json` body keyed by the `IdentityError` code (for example `ConcurrencyFailure`). Successful requests are unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

* [ ] When `SetTwoFactorEnabledAsync` returns a failed `IdentityResult`, `/manage/2fa` returns a validation problem containing the error code, for both the enable and disable paths.
* [ ] A functional test in `src/Identity/test/Identity.FunctionalTests/MapIdentityApiTests.cs` uses a `UserManager` that returns `ConcurrencyFailure` from `SetTwoFactorEnabledAsync` and asserts both paths; the test fails without the fix and passes with it.
* [ ] Existing 2FA tests (`CanEnableAndLoginWithTwoFactor`, `CanLoginWithRecoveryCodeAndDisableTwoFactor`) continue to pass.
* [ ] Decision recorded for `ResetAuthenticatorKeyAsync` and recovery code generation handling.

Issues.Title: RemoteAuthenticationHandler ignores TicketReceivedContext.Fail() and proceeds to sign-in
Issues.Body:
## Summary

`RemoteAuthenticationHandler` ignores a failure result set through `TicketReceivedContext.Fail(...)` in the `TicketReceived` event. The handler continues to `SignInAsync` as if the event had completed normally, so the failure signal has no effect.

## What is wrong

* `RemoteAuthenticationContext<TOptions>.Fail(...)` is public API on the context passed to `OnTicketReceived`. It is documented only as "Indicates that authentication failed."
* After `Events.TicketReceived` runs, `HandleRequestCoreAsync` inspects only `Result.Handled` and `Result.Skipped`. `Result.Failure` is never examined, so a failed result falls through to sign-in and redirect.
* This is inconsistent with the same method's handling of `RemoteFailure`, which throws `AuthenticationFailureException` when `Result.Failure` is set, and with OpenID Connect `RemoteSignOut`, which also acts on `Result.Failure`.
* `TicketReceived` is invoked outside the `try/catch` that wraps `HandleRemoteAuthenticateAsync`, so only an exception thrown by user code, or `HandleResponse()` / `SkipHandler()`, currently prevents sign-in from this event.

## Why it matters (defense in depth)

* Correctness: a public API whose name and documentation say "authentication failed" is silently a no-op in this event. Apps that use it to enforce an application-level admission policy on an external identity get no enforcement.
* Hardening: the remote authentication handler is the boundary between an external identity provider and the local sign-in scheme. Failure signals raised by application code at that boundary should fail closed.
* Existing tests cover `SkipHandler()` and `HandleResponse()` for `OnTicketReceived`, but not `Fail(...)`, so the gap is not locked by any test.
* Applies to all remote schemes built on `RemoteAuthenticationHandler` (OAuth and derived providers, OpenID Connect, WS-Federation, and others). The same code is present on `main` and on `release/8.0`, `release/9.0`, and `release/10.0`.

## Affected code

* src/Security/Authentication/Core/src/RemoteAuthenticationHandler.cs:162-176 - result handling after `Events.TicketReceived`; no `Result.Failure` branch
* src/Security/Authentication/Core/src/RemoteAuthenticationHandler.cs:178 - `SignInAsync` reached when the result is a failure
* src/Security/Authentication/Core/src/RemoteAuthenticationHandler.cs:126-141 - existing `RemoteFailure` handling that already honors `Result.Failure`
* src/Security/Authentication/Core/src/Events/RemoteAuthenticationContext.cs:48-58 - `Fail(Exception)` and `Fail(string)` that set the failure result
* src/Security/Authentication/Core/src/Events/RemoteAuthenticationEvents.cs:21-39 - `OnTicketReceived` / `TicketReceived`

## Recommended fix

**Selected approach (servicing and main):** add a `Result.Failure` branch after the existing `Handled` and `Skipped` checks that throws `AuthenticationFailureException` before `SignInAsync` is called, mirroring the `RemoteFailure` handling. For example, use the message "An error was returned from the TicketReceived event." with `ticketContext.Result.Failure` as the inner exception. No public API change, so no `PublicAPI.*.txt` update or API review is needed.

**Alternatives considered:**

* Route the failure through `Events.RemoteFailure` so applications can render a custom error page. This gives a better experience but requires restructuring the shared failure block and the `Debug.Assert(ticket != null)` flow, changes event ordering and logging, and has a larger backport risk. It is reasonable as a follow-up on `main`.
* Leave behavior unchanged and document that `Fail(...)` is ignored in this event. Not chosen: the API reads as a rejection signal, and sibling handler paths honor it.
* Also honor `context.Success()` and other result shapes in this event. Out of scope for this fix.

**Compatibility and migration:**

* Apps that call `Fail(...)` in `OnTicketReceived` today and rely on it being ignored will start failing the remote login. This is a behavior change on servicing branches, so call it out in the PR description and release notes. Consider whether an `AppContext` opt-out switch is warranted, following precedent for similar servicing fixes.
* The supported ways to stop sign-in from this event remain `HandleResponse()` and `SkipHandler()`; their behavior is unchanged.
* The same hunk should backport cleanly to `release/8.0`, `release/9.0`, and `release/10.0`; the surrounding logic is identical on those branches.
* The existing XML documentation ("Indicates that authentication failed.") is accurate once the handler honors the failure, so no documentation change is required.

## Acceptance criteria

* [ ] Calling `Fail(...)` from `OnTicketReceived` prevents `SignInAsync` from being called, so no sign-in cookie is issued for the sign-in scheme.
* [ ] The failure surfaces as `AuthenticationFailureException` carrying the original failure as its inner exception.
* [ ] Regression tests in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Test` cover an OAuth-derived handler (for example the Google tests) and OpenID Connect, next to the existing `OnTicketReceived_Skip_*` and `OnTicketReceived_Handled_*` tests. Each test fails without the fix for the expected reason and passes with it.
* [ ] `Handled` and `Skipped` behavior for `TicketReceived` is unchanged.
* [ ] The behavior change is noted in the PR description and servicing notes, and the opt-out decision is recorded.
* [ ] The fix is backported to `release/8.0`, `release/9.0`, and `release/10.0`.

Issues.Title: Migrate Blazor E2E tests to Components.Testing
Issues.Body:
## Summary

We introduced `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Testing` (#65958, #66394, #68289) to provide a modern, Playwright based end-to-end testing infrastructure for Blazor applications. This issue tracks incrementally migrating our existing Selenium-based E2E test suite (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests`) to `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Testing`, cleaning up our `testassets`, and evolving the library into a public package and agent skill that Blazor developers can use to test their own applications.

## Goals

1. **Incrementally migrate existing E2E tests to `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Testing`:**
   - Replace legacy Selenium tests with readable, fast Playwright tests using `ServerFixture`, YARP proxy routing, and cross-process service overrides (following a developer experience similar to `WebApplicationFactory`).
   - Enable running E2E tests across multiple browsers and make it easy for developers and coding agents to run and filter E2E tests locally.
2. **Avoid test-logic flakiness by design:**
   - Tests migrated to the new infrastructure must be deterministic and not rely on arbitrary sleeps and polling.
   - Instead of one-off hacks in individual tests, we will build first-class synchronization primitives, lifecycle hooks, and readiness gates into the framework and testing library (for example, observing prerendered DOM state before interactive activation, waiting for Blazor runtime startup, enhanced navigation completion, or interactive handoff).
3. **Standardize framework test hooks for public consumption:**
   - As we migrate tests that currently rely on internal workarounds to inspect or gate framework state, replace those workarounds with clean, supported entry points and diagnostic channels.
   - Because `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Testing` is intended to ship as a supported package for Blazor developers, the primitives we add should be designed for public consumption.
4. **Clean up and reorganize `testassets` and test structure:**
   - Re-evaluate and simplify the existing E2E `testassets` projects that have accumulated overlapping scenarios over time so they are easier to navigate and debug.
   - Support running selected test subsets across different hosting configurations (such as Server vs. WebAssembly) and isolated process configurations (such as different `AppContext` switches or Native AOT via #68289).
   - Improve CI and Helix execution partitioning (for example, attribute-driven test groups/traits and Helix job generation similar to `Wasm.Build.Tests` in `dotnet/runtime`).
5. **Better diagnostics, CI reliability, and developer/agent ergonomics:**
   - Leverage built-in Playwright tracing and structured diagnostics on failure.
   - Keep overall suite execution time low while separating genuine infrastructure failures (recoverable via selective test re-runs) from test-logic races.
   - Ship a reusable E2E testing skill and guidance so customers and agents can adopt `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Testing` in their own projects.

## Open Questions / Further Exploration

- How to best structure multi-environment and isolated `AppContext` test permutations in MSBuild and Helix.
- Whether and how to extend the testing model to cover `BlazorWebView` / Hybrid scenarios (WinForms, WPF, MAUI).
- Integration with CI selective retry / Test Monitor for transient machine or network failures.

# Fix QuickGrid paginator page-change announcements

Add polite, atomic announcements for QuickGrid paginator page changes.

## Description

Add `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"` to the Paginator's page-status text so assistive technology can announce the complete updated status, such as “Page 2 of 3”, without moving keyboard focus.

This applies to both anchor- and button-based navigation, including paginators with custom summaries. Visual appearance and pagination behavior remain unchanged.

Addresses dotnet/aspnetcore-scenario-tests#153.

## Customer Impact

The Paginator currently updates its visible page status without requesting a screen-reader announcement. Users may not know which page is displayed without manually locating and reading the status.

## Why Backport

The affected Paginator implementation ships in .NET 11. Backporting makes page-status updates available for automatic announcement to screen-reader users.

## Regression?

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

Longstanding accessibility gap present in the original productized QuickGrid implementation.

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [ ] Medium
- [x] Low

Scoped to two ARIA attributes in both navigation modes. No visual, pagination logic, or public API changes.

## Verification

- [x] Manual (required)
- [x] Automated

Browser before/after validation completed on #70017. All seven targeted Selenium cases passed.

## Packaging changes reviewed?

- [ ] Yes
- [ ] No
- [x] N/A

No packaging changes.

Issues.Title: Fix Paginator RTL navigation alignment
Issues.Body:
Use a logical margin to align Paginator navigation consistently in LTR and RTL.

## Description

Replace `margin-left: auto` with `margin-inline-start: auto` in the shared
Paginator navigation styles.

The physical left margin correctly separates the summary and navigation in LTR,
but leaves navigation beside the summary instead of at the opposite edge in RTL.
The logical margin preserves existing LTR behavior and places navigation at
inline-end in RTL.

Add AbortLink to cancel browser operations with a CancellationToken

## Description

This is the prototype for the design discussion in #70044. It adds the internal `AbortLink` and its tests. The public API does not change, and no family uses `AbortLink` yet. The first one will be Fetch (#69882). I keep this as a draft until the design is agreed.

### AbortLink

`AbortLink.CreateAsync(IJSRuntime, CancellationToken)` creates a browser `AbortController` with `InvokeConstructorAsync`, reads its `signal` as an object reference, and registers a callback on the token that calls `abort()`. A family passes `Signal` to the browser operation, and calls the operation through `IJSRuntime` with `CancellationToken.None`. The issue explains why.

A few details are worth a look.

- The two setup calls (the constructor and `signal`) use the overloads without a token, so they keep the default interop timeout. Only the browser operation itself runs with `CancellationToken.None`.
- `CreateAsync` returns `null` for a token that cannot be canceled, so a call without a token costs nothing. For a token that is already canceled, it throws before any interop call.
- If the token is canceled while the setup calls run, `CreateAsync` disposes both references and throws, before it registers the callback. If the token is canceled just before `Register`, `Register` runs the callback at once, so the abort is not lost.
- The callback ignores any failure of `abort()`, such as a closed circuit. It runs on the thread that cancels the token and changes no state, so it needs no lock.
- `DisposeAsync` removes the callback first. `CancellationTokenRegistration.DisposeAsync` waits for a callback that is running, so no `abort()` goes to a disposed reference. It then disposes the two references. `JSObjectReference.DisposeAsync` already ignores `JSDisconnectedException`, so `DisposeAsync` has no `catch`.
- `CreateCanceledException` builds the `OperationCanceledException` that a family throws when its interop call fails after the token was canceled. It keeps the browser error as `InnerException`.

The csproj gets `InternalsVisibleTo` for the unit tests and for `PlatformTestApp.Client`, because the demo page calls the internal type. `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.csproj` has the same for `BasicTestApp`.

### Tests

- `AbortLinkTest` has 9 unit tests with a recording fake. The fake leaves the overloads with a token unimplemented, so a call that passes a token fails the test. The tests cover the token that cannot be canceled, the canceled token, cancellation during setup, a failing setup, an abort that fails, disposal, and `CreateCanceledException`.
- `AbortLinkTests` has 3 E2E tests in both render modes. `AbortLinkDemo.razor` calls `fetch` the way a family would, and the test app server has endpoints that record whether the browser aborted each request. The tests check the record on the server. They cover a request that is left alone until the token is canceled, an abort before the headers and while the body is read, and a token that is already canceled, for which no request is sent. The page uses the result marker of the other E2E tests.
- Unit tests 43 of 43 pass, and the E2E tests 3 of 3 pass with `dotnet run`. All 9 E2E tests of the package pass from the output of `dotnet publish`. When I removed the `abort()` call from `AbortLink`, `AbortLink_AbortsTheRequestInTheBrowserWhenTheTokenIsCanceled` failed, so the test depends on the real abort. The E2E tests run in Chromium only.

### What I checked in other browsers

Before this PR, I checked the idea in a scratch app that is not in this PR. It calls `fetch` through plain `IJSRuntime` calls, and its server records whether the browser aborted each request. I ran it in Interactive Server and WebAssembly, in Chromium, Firefox, and the WebKit build that Playwright ships for Windows. The results were the same in all six.

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Token passed to `IJSRuntime` only | .NET throws `TaskCanceledException`, but the server request runs to completion. |
| `abort()` while waiting for the headers | `fetch` rejects at once and the server sees the abort. |
| `abort()` after `fetch` resolved, while `text()` reads the body | `text()` rejects and the server sees the abort. |
| Signal that is already aborted | `fetch` rejects at once and no request reaches the server. |
| `abort()` from `token.Register` in Interactive Server | Works, also when the callback runs outside the circuit's sync context. |
| Error text of an abort | Chromium "signal is aborted without reason" (and "The user aborted a request." while reading the body), Firefox "The operation was aborted.", WebKit "Fetch is aborted". WebKit ignores a reason passed to `abort()`. |

The error text differs by browser, so `AbortLink` never reads it. A family decides by `token.IsCancellationRequested`.

Contributes to #70044

Issues.Title: How Components.Platform should cancel browser operations with a CancellationToken
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Some browser APIs take an `AbortSignal`, such as `fetch()`, `locks.request()`, and `credentials.get()`. The porting skill maps it to a `CancellationToken`, but a token given to `IJSRuntime` does not stop the browser operation. I propose one internal type for all families. When a browser operation starts, it creates a browser `AbortController` with JS interop and passes its signal to the browser operation. It also registers a callback on the `CancellationToken` (`token.Register`). When the token is canceled, the callback calls `abort()` on the controller through JS interop, and the browser stops the operation.

**Fetch (#69882) needs this decision first.** `FetchAsync` cannot cancel a request until we agree how the token reaches the browser. The answer also decides who owns the `AbortLink` after `fetch()` returns, so it shapes `Response`. I would like to settle it before the Fetch design is fixed.

## Motivation and goals

The porting skill already says that real cancellation needs a JS-side `AbortController` that .NET aborts through interop. It does not say how, and three families need it.

- **Fetch (#69882).** Without cancellation, an app cannot stop a request that the user no longer wants, such as a search box that sends a request for each key. It is also the hardest case, because the signal stays bound to the `Response` body after `fetch()` returns.
- **Web Locks (#69876).** To cancel a pending `locks.request()`.
- **Credentials (#69880).** To cancel a pending `credentials.get()` or `create()`.

Fetch can ship without a token, and a token can be added later without a breaking change. But a `fetch` that cannot be canceled is a weak API for the most common browser call, and the `Response` design depends on this answer. So I see this as a blocker for the cancellation part of Fetch.

A token given to `IJSRuntime` only stops .NET from waiting. In my test, a `fetch` canceled after 500 ms still ran for 2 seconds on the server. A `Response` that the browser returns later is registered on the JS side, and then dropped by `EndInvokeJS`, so nothing disposes it. The default interop timeout takes the same path.

Goals.

- Canceling the token stops the browser operation, before and after data starts to arrive.
- The caller gets `OperationCanceledException` with its own token, the same in every browser.
- No extra cost without a token, and no JS of our own.

## In scope

- An internal type that links a token to a browser `AbortController`, for every family with an `AbortSignal`, and the rules for starting such browser operations through `IJSRuntime`.

## Out of scope

- A public `AbortController` and `AbortSignal` projection (#69883). It can be added later next to the token, and needs #69924 and #69922 first.
- The public shape of Fetch (#69882).

## Risks / unknowns

- **Two extra JS interop round trips** for each browser operation that has a cancelable token, to create the controller and to read its `signal`. A helper in the JS bridge of #69922 could make it one. I have not tried that.
- **Memory leak when the circuit ends during a JS interop call, with a token that outlives the circuit.** `AbortLink` registers a callback on the caller's token, and removes it when it is disposed. The JS interop call that starts the browser operation (such as `fetch`) uses `CancellationToken.None`. So if the circuit ends while that JS interop call is pending, its `await` never completes, as with any interop call made with `CancellationToken.None` today, and the `AbortLink` is never disposed. The callback then stays on the token's `CancellationTokenSource`, which keeps the `AbortLink` and, through it, the circuit's `JSRuntime` alive until the source is canceled. This happens only with a token that outlives the circuit, such as one from a singleton. Component tokens and timeouts created for one operation are not affected. I expect to resolve it on top of the per-scope `FeatureContext` of #69993. `AbortLink` can then be tied to the scope, and the scope can dispose the `AbortLink` instances that are still open when the circuit ends.

## Examples

Fetch is only an example here. Its real shape is up to #69882.

```csharp
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));

var response = await Browser.Window.FetchAsync("/api/orders", new RequestInit { Method = "GET" }, cts.Token);
var text = await response.TextAsync();
```

If the token is canceled while the request is sent, while the browser waits for the headers, or while it reads the body, the browser aborts the request and the app gets `OperationCanceledException` with `cts.Token`.

## Detailed design

```csharp
internal sealed class AbortLink : IAsyncDisposable
{
    // null for a token that cannot be canceled; throws for a token that is already canceled.
    public static ValueTask<AbortLink?> CreateAsync(IJSRuntime jsRuntime, CancellationToken cancellationToken);

    public IJSObjectReference Signal { get; }

    public static OperationCanceledException CreateCanceledException(Exception innerException, CancellationToken cancellationToken);

    public ValueTask DisposeAsync();
}
```

An `AbortLink` holds three things. They are the references to the JS `AbortController` and its `signal`, and the callback registered on the token. `CreateAsync` calls `new AbortController()` with `InvokeConstructorAsync`, reads its `signal` as an object reference, and registers a callback on the token that calls `abort()`. `DisposeAsync` removes the callback from the token first, then disposes the two references.

A family calls the browser like this.

```csharp
var abortLink = await AbortLink.CreateAsync(jsRuntime, cancellationToken);
try
{
    // CancellationToken.None also turns off the interop timeout. Only the `AbortLink` cancels the request.
    var response = await jsRuntime.InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>(
        "fetch", CancellationToken.None, [url, new { signal = abortLink?.Signal }]);
    // ...
}
catch (JSException ex) when (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    throw AbortLink.CreateCanceledException(ex, cancellationToken);
}
```

Rules.

1. **Never give the token to `IJSRuntime`.** Start the browser operation through `IJSRuntime` with `CancellationToken.None`. This is an exception to the skill rule "When the caller passes no `CancellationToken`, call the `IJSRuntime` overload without a token", so the skill would get a rule for it.
2. **Decide by the token, not by the error.** If the JS interop call fails after the token was canceled, throw `OperationCanceledException` with the token and keep the browser error as `InnerException`. This includes a network error that races with the abort. If the JS interop call succeeds just before the abort reaches the browser, dispose the result and throw as well.
3. **Keep the `AbortLink` until the operation can no longer be aborted, then call its `DisposeAsync`.** That releases the two JS references and removes the callback from the token. For most operations, that is when the JS interop call returns. For `fetch`, the signal also covers reading the response body, so the `AbortLink` must outlive `fetch()`. The `Response` holds it, and disposes it when the body has been read, when the fetch fails, or when the `Response` is disposed.
4. **Body methods take no token.** `text()` and the other body methods have no `AbortSignal` in Web IDL, so `TextAsync()` and the like take none. The token given to `FetchAsync` also cancels reading the body.

### What I verified

I called `fetch` through plain `IJSRuntime` calls in a test app whose server records whether the browser aborted each request. I ran it in Interactive Server and WebAssembly, in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with the same results in all six. A token given to `IJSRuntime` leaves the server request running to completion. An `abort()` through `AbortLink` stops it, both while the browser waits for the headers and while it reads the body.

A prototype of `AbortLink` is in #70045, with unit tests and E2E tests in both render modes. The details are there.

### Considered alternatives

- **Take a public `AbortSignal` instead of a token.** Closer to Web IDL, but .NET code already uses tokens, and the library could not tell whether a failure was a cancellation. It needs caller-owned objects and events first, and can still be added next to the token later.
- **Translate the error by its name or message.** The text differs by browser, and `JSException` does not carry the error name.

### Open questions

None.

Issues.Title: Fix cross-site antiforgery cookie resets in Blazor SSR
Issues.Body:
# Fix cross-site antiforgery cookie resets in Blazor SSR

Prevent form-free cross-site SSR navigation from resetting antiforgery cookies.

## Description

A cross-site navigation can omit the existing SameSite=Strict antiforgery cookie. Streaming SSR currently generates a replacement cookie before determining whether the destination contains a form. This invalidates a form already open in another tab, causing its next submission to return 400.

This change:
- Waits for rendering to finish on cross-site GET requests when the default endpoint antiforgery provider and middleware require a new cookie.
- Tracks interactive components actually rendered, rather than relying on application-wide configured render modes.
- Prevents form-free static pages from generating a replacement cookie merely to persist component state.
- Preserves token generation for forms rendered asynchronously and for interactive components that may require tokens after activation.

Cookie defaults and antiforgery validation are unchanged. No public API or JavaScript changes are introduced.

### Behavior trade-off

Affected cross-site requests wait for rendering to finish before response headers are sent. Other requests retain streaming behavior.

This delays initial content on affected requests and can prevent an indefinite streaming response from producing initial output. The change does not prevent cookie replacement when the destination itself requires a form or an interactive token. This trade-off is documented in the Components contributor guidance.

### Regression coverage

Three new browser tests cover:
1. Cross-site navigation to a form-free streaming page preserves the existing cookie and original form token, and the original form submits successfully.
2. Cross-site navigation supports a form rendered after asynchronous work.
3. Direct navigation still streams initial content before asynchronous work completes and preserves the original form's usability.

The tests use a real cross-site link and a controlled asynchronous gate, rather than injected headers or arbitrary sleeps.

### Validation

Recorded local validation on Windows/Kestrel:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Focused Endpoints/rendering unit tests | 89 passed; no failures or skips |
| Focused Selenium tests, including existing controls | 8 passed; no failures or skips |
| Sample and Selenium project builds | Passed with 0 warnings and 0 errors |
| Canonical browser reproduction before the fix | 400 in 10/10 runs; cookie replaced |
| Canonical browser reproduction after the fix | 200 in 10/10 runs; cookie preserved |

Red/green verification of the three new tests:

| Scenario | Without fix | With fix |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-site, form-free streaming destination | Failed: original form POST returned 400 | Passed |
| Cross-site, asynchronously rendered form | Passed | Passed |
| Direct-navigation streaming control | Passed | Passed |

Commands used for focused automated validation:

```powershell

$unitFilter = 'FullyQualifiedName~RazorComponentEndpointInvokerTest|FullyQualifiedName~RazorComponentResultTest|FullyQualifiedName~EndpointHtmlRendererTest|FullyQualifiedName~EndpointAntiforgeryStateProviderTest'

    --no-restore --filter $unitFilter -v:q `
    -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -m:1 -nr:false
# Passed: 89 tests.

dotnet build .\src\Components\test\E2ETest\Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests.csproj `
    --no-restore -v:q -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -m:1 -nr:false
# Passed: 0 warnings, 0 errors.

$env:TEST_CHROME_BINARY = 'C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe'
```

Bound nested-group recursion depth in Negotiate LdapAdapter

## Description

Hi! This follows the approach suggested in #69611. Thanks for writing it up in so much detail, that made it easy to pick up.

`GetGroups` now gets the current depth and stops going further up once it reaches `MaxNestedGroupDepth`, which is an internal constant set to 32. The direct group counts as depth 0. Whatever was collected up to that point is kept. No public API changes.

When the limit is hit, one warning is logged for the whole resolution, not one per group. It only includes the user name and the limit, no group names. To make that testable, I moved the loop over the user's direct groups into a small `GetGroupClaims` helper.

The visited-set check still runs before the depth check, so cycles are skipped like before and aren't reported as truncation.

I left the existing `return` for already processed groups alone on purpose. Switching it to `continue` would change which claims some directories get back, so it felt better as its own change. Happy to send a follow-up if you'd like.

I also added a short remark to the `LdapSettings.IgnoreNestedGroups` docs about the limit.

### Tests

I used the same `LdapConnection` subclass plus the reflection helper for building responses that #69955 uses. Whichever of the two gets merged second can just reuse the helper from the other one, and I'm happy to handle the merge on my side.

New tests:
* no nesting, one level below the limit, and exactly at the limit: the whole chain is resolved and nothing is logged
* above the limit: claims up to the limit are returned, the next group is never read, and one warning is logged
* two direct groups, both over the limit: still just one warning
* a circular reference: it terminates without extra reads and without a warning

All 105 tests in `Negotiate.Test` pass locally. When I disabled only the depth check, just the two over-the-limit tests failed.

Fixes #69611

Issues.Title: Don't expire infinite Kestrel timeouts on the next heartbeat
Issues.Body:
# Don't expire infinite Kestrel timeouts on the next heartbeat

Make `Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan` actually disable `KeepAliveTimeout` and `RequestHeadersTimeout`.

## Description

`KestrelServerLimits` stores an infinite timeout as `TimeSpan.MaxValue`, which `ToTicks` turns into `long.MaxValue`. `TimeoutControl.AssignTimeout` then adds the last timestamp and the heartbeat interval to it. The sum wraps negative and the timeout fires on the next heartbeat. So an idle connection with an infinite keep-alive closes after about a second, and incomplete headers with an infinite header timeout get a 408. HTTP/2 goes through the same code.

The expiration is now clamped to `long.MaxValue` on overflow, the same way `Http3Connection` already handles its stream timeouts.

Added a `TimeoutControl` test and functional tests for both limits.

Fixes #69692

# Reject chunk sizes larger than Int32.MaxValue with 400

Return 400 instead of 500 when a chunk size overflows.

## Description

`CalculateChunkSize` turned the `OverflowException` into a plain `IOException`, so a chunk size like `80000000` escaped to the app and ended up as a 500. Every other bad chunk size is already a 400. It now throws `BadChunkSizeData` like the non-hex case.

Updated the existing test that expected the `IOException` and added the overflow cases to `InvalidLengthResultsIn400`.

Fixes #69819

Issues.Title: Reject HTTP/1.1 request lines with no space before the version
Issues.Body:
# Reject HTTP/1.1 request lines with no space before the version

Return 400 for request lines like `GET /aHTTP/1.1` again.

## Description

Since #51535, `TryParseRequestLine` finds the end of the target with `IndexOfAny`. When nothing matches, `offset` stays at `targetStart + 1`, the next byte is consumed as the separator, and the version check still passes. So `GET /aHTTP/1.1` is accepted with `Path == "/"`, while 8.0 returned 400.

The parser now returns the invalid request line error when it can't find the end of the target. Added the shape to the invalid request line data and a test with bare LF terminators allowed.

Fixes #69857

Issues.Title: [API Proposal] Capture pending JSRuntime calls for deferred failure
Issues.Body:
## Background and Motivation

Originating issue: #67479. Implementation: #68714 (head 95df2ccc146a014b365cdec4dd8266d00f026155).

When SignalR closes a Blazor Server connection before a JavaScript interop result reaches the server, pending JSRuntime.InvokeAsync operations can remain pending until cancellation or the default timeout. The original report clarified that this is a roughly 60-second wait rather than a permanent deadlock.

Derived runtimes need to capture calls belonging to the previous connection before transferring to a replacement client, then fail those calls outside the circuit registry lock. This proposal exposes the protected helper used by the implementation.

## Usage Examples

RemoteJSRuntime wraps the helper:

```csharp
internal virtual Action CapturePendingTasksForDisconnect()
{
    return CapturePendingTasks(new JSDisconnectedException(
        "JavaScript interop calls cannot complete because the circuit disconnected."));
}
```

During an active reconnect, CircuitRegistry marks the old client disconnected, captures pending calls, and transfers the replacement client. The returned action is invoked outside the registry lock. Calls created by the replacement connection are not part of the captured set.

## Proposed API

```diff
namespace Microsoft.JSInterop
{
    public abstract partial class JSRuntime : IJSRuntime, System.IDisposable
    {
+       protected System.Action CapturePendingTasks(System.Exception exception);
    }
}
```

The helper rejects a null exception, removes the captured pending calls and their cancellation registrations, and returns an action that fails those calls with the supplied exception and disposes the captured registrations. Capture and invocation dispatch share a synchronization boundary.

## Alternative Designs

The earlier implementation completed pending calls through disconnect cleanup after client transfer. Review identified that a replacement connection could create new calls before cleanup ran. The current capture-then-complete shape separates selecting old calls from completing them, allowing completion outside the registry lock.

## Risks

Review identified two correctness constraints: stale disconnect cleanup must not fault replacement-connection calls, and an invocation captured as failed must not subsequently dispatch to the replacement client. The implementation adds regression tests for reconnect capture ordering and in-flight dispatch. Stream startup failure must also remove the constructed RemoteJSDataStream registration.

The helper adds a protected API surface and synchronization around invocation registration/dispatch. API naming and the returned-action contract require review.

## Review ownership

Proposal and implementation author: @imsouvik. A maintainer champion and API meeting representative have not yet been arranged; please advise on ownership before scheduling review.

## Source Justifications

- Timeout rather than permanent deadlock — #67479: "What occurs is a 60-second pause, followed by a TaskCanceledException".
- Pending calls survive disconnection — #67479 discussion: "Blazor isn't canceling any pending JSRuntime.InvokeAsync calls if the connection closes".
- Public API shape — #68714 baseline: `Microsoft.JSInterop.JSRuntime.CapturePendingTasks(System.Exception! exception) -> System.Action!`.
- Deferred completion — #68714 XML documentation: "Captures all pending asynchronous JavaScript calls so they can be failed with the specified exception" and "An action that fails the captured calls."
- Synchronization — #68714 implementation: "Capture and dispatch share this lock so a captured call cannot begin dispatch after capture returns."
- Reconnect risk — #68714 review: "make the cleanup connection-generation-aware so a stale disconnect cannot sweep replacement-generation calls, while avoiding completion of user tasks under the registry lock."
- Dispatch risk — #68714 review: "allowing side-effecting JavaScript to run even though completePendingTasks() faults the .NET task".
- Stream cleanup — #68714 implementation: `remoteJSDataStream.Dispose();` in the startup exception path.

Issues.Title: RedisOutputCacheStore force reconnect can release the current connection instead of the failed one
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

Hi! I was looking at the force reconnect path in `RedisOutputCacheStore` and noticed something that I think is a leftover from when the output cache store was split out.

With force reconnect enabled (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Caching.StackExchangeRedis.UseForceReconnect`), `OnRedisError` clears the shared connection with:

```csharp
ReleaseConnection(Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref _cache, null, cache));
```

Since `Interlocked.CompareExchange` returns the value `_cache` had before the call, if another caller has already reconnected in the meantime, this returns the new connection, and that one gets released while `_cache` still points to it. The comment above the line describes the intended behavior (only clear the field if it still holds the failed connection), so I believe this is just the older version of the line.

`RedisCache` had the same line, and it was updated in #52608 to only release when `ReferenceEquals(tmp, cache)`. It looks like `RedisOutputCacheStore` was split into its own package in #50457 shortly before that, so the update didn't make it over. Otherwise `OnRedisError` is identical in both files.

When this happens, `ConnectAsync` keeps returning the disposed connection from `_cache`, so every later call fails with `ObjectDisposedException`. Since `OnRedisError` only reacts to `RedisConnectionException` and `SocketException`, the store doesn't recover on its own. The repro below shows this with real `ConnectionMultiplexer` instances.

### Expected Behavior

I think `OnRedisError` should mirror `RedisCache` here and only release the connection it actually removed from `_cache`:

```csharp
var tmp = Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref _cache, null, cache);
if (ReferenceEquals(tmp, cache))
{
    ReleaseConnection(tmp);
}
```

### Steps To Reproduce

I haven't hit this in practice, I found it while reading the code. The interleaving I have in mind:

1. Requests A and B both fail on connection X and both pass the reconnect timing checks.
2. A swaps X out of `_cache` and releases it.
3. Request C calls `ConnectAsync`, finds `_cache` empty and stores a new connection Y.
4. B runs `CompareExchange(ref _cache, null, X)`. It fails, returns Y, and `ReleaseConnection(Y)` closes the connection `_cache` still references.

The window is pretty narrow (B would have to stall between its checks and the exchange for as long as the reconnect takes), so it's unlikely to show up often. When it does, though, it would most likely be during a Redis outage under load, which is exactly when force reconnect is needed.

### Exceptions (if any)

`ObjectDisposedException` from every request after the late `OnRedisError` call (see the repro output).

### .NET Version

main (ceb0eec). The line is unchanged since the package was created in #50457.

### Anything else?

Related, but I think separate: #55898 (factory-provided connection disposed on force reconnect in RedisCache) and #69849 (GC loop ignores disposal).

I'd be happy to open a PR with the fix if that sounds good. Thanks!

Issues.Body:
# Cancel pending cookie renewal when the principal is rejected

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Don't renew the cookie when ValidatePrincipal rejects the principal

## Description

`CookieAuthenticationHandler.HandleAuthenticateAsync` runs the sliding expiration check before `ValidatePrincipal`, so the refresh ticket is cloned before any per-request changes to the principal. When `ValidatePrincipal` then rejected the principal, the handler returned `NoPrincipal` but kept the pending refresh. Unless sign-in or sign-out was also called in that request, `FinishResponseAsync` still wrote a renewed cookie for the rejected ticket, and with a `SessionStore` it also called `ITicketStore.RenewAsync` for it.

Changes:

- The rejection branch in `HandleAuthenticateAsync` now clears the pending refresh (`_shouldRefresh`, `_refreshTicket` and the two refresh timestamps) before returning `NoPrincipal`.
- The snapshot taken before validation and the successful validation path are unchanged. `RejectPrincipal()` still doesn't sign out, so the existing cookie and stored session are left as they are and keep their original expiration. An explicit `SignOutAsync` still deletes the cookie and removes the stored session.

Tests:

- `CookieTests.CookieNotRenewedWhenRejectedByValidator`, for both cookie-only and session store configurations with sliding expiration on. It rejects once before a renewal is due, once after it's due (no `Set-Cookie`, stored ticket not replaced), and then rejects and signs out (deletion cookie, stored session removed). Without the handler change both cases fail on the request where the renewal is due: a renewed cookie is written, and with the session store `RenewAsync` also replaces the stored ticket with one that expires later.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Test` (714 passed, 3 skipped in source) and `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.InMemory.Test` (226 passed) pass locally.

### Compatibility

The only observable change is that the response for a rejected principal no longer carries a renewed cookie or triggers `RenewAsync`. There's no public API change, and the ticket format and data protection purposes are the same, so existing cookies and stored tickets keep working.

`SecurityStampValidator` already signs out when the stamp check fails, so the usual Identity flow behaves the same. When `SecurityStampValidatorOptions.OnRefreshingPrincipal` sets `NewPrincipal` to null, authentication fails without a sign-out, and that path now skips the renewal as well.

I only targeted main. Whether this should go to release/8.0 or release/10.0 is a servicing call, so I've left that to you. Happy to file a breaking change note if you think it needs one.

Fixes #69701

Issues.Title: Kestrel can deadlock registering a certificate file watch (CertificatePathWatcher._metadataLock vs CompositeChangeToken._callbackLock)
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

With a certificate configured by path (Kestrel:Certificates:Default:Path), Kestrel can deadlock while it registers the file watch: at start (BindAsync), or on a configuration reload that points the certificate at a new directory (RebindAsync). On macOS no file has to change. A start that deadlocks never binds. A rebind that deadlocks holds Kestrel's bind semaphore, so later rebinds and StopAsync wait forever.

### Expected Behavior

Kestrel starts, or rebinds, with the certificate, whatever thread the file watcher's timer runs on. If a change to the certificate file arrives while the watch is being registered, Kestrel either picks it up or ignores it, and nothing hangs.

### Steps To Reproduce

Repro project: https://github.com/BrianWhy/kestrel-cert-watch-deadlock

It is the ASP.NET Core Empty template (`dotnet new web`) with only `Program.cs` changed. `Program.cs` writes a self-signed certificate to a temporary directory once and never changes it. It then starts and stops Kestrel in a loop, with that certificate configured by path (`Kestrel:Certificates:Default:Path`).

1. `dotnet run -c Release`
2. When it prints `Start <n> hung. Stacks: dotnet-stack report -p <pid>`, run that command in another terminal (`dotnet tool install -g dotnet-stack`).

On ASP.NET Core 10.0.13 / .NET 10.0.13, macOS 27.0.1 arm64, 14 cores, it hung at start 872 after 100 s, and at start 3,604 after 6 min 35 s. On 10.0.12 the same project hung at start 1,930 after about 4 minutes and at start 4,456 after about 10 minutes.

<details><summary>Program.cs</summary>

```csharp
// Starts and stops Kestrel in a loop with a certificate configured by path. The file is written once and never changed.
using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates;

var pfx = Path.Combine(Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory().FullName, "cert.pfx");
File.WriteAllBytes(pfx, new CertificateRequest("CN=localhost", RSA.Create(2048), HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.Pkcs1)
    .CreateSelfSigned(DateTimeOffset.Now, DateTimeOffset.Now.AddDays(1)).Export(X509ContentType.Pfx));

for (int n = 1; ; n++)
{
    var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(["--urls=https://127.0.0.1:0", $"--Kestrel:Certificates:Default:Path={pfx}"]);
    builder.Logging.ClearProviders();
    var app = builder.Build();
    if (!Task.Run(async () => { await app.StartAsync(); await app.StopAsync(); }).Wait(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10)))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Start {n} hung. Stacks: dotnet-stack report -p {Environment.ProcessId}");
        Console.ReadLine();
        return;
    }
    await app.DisposeAsync();
}
```

</details>

### Exceptions (if any)

None: the start hangs. These are the two deadlocked threads, from `dotnet-stack report` against the repro on 10.0.13 at the hang. Two samples 6 s apart showed the same two threads.

```
thread-pool thread: PhysicalFilesWatcher's polling timer
  System.Threading.Lock.TryEnterSlow                                    <- waits for _metadataLock
  Kestrel.Core.Internal.CertificatePathWatcher.OnChange(String)
  Primitives.ChangeToken+ChangeTokenRegistration`1.OnChangeTokenFired()
  Primitives.ChangeToken+ChangeTokenRegistration`1+<>c.<RegisterChangeTokenCallback>b__7_0(Object)
  System.Threading.CancellationTokenSource.ExecuteCallbackHandlers(Boolean)
  Primitives.CompositeChangeToken.OnChange(Object)                      <- holds _callbackLock
  System.Threading.CancellationTokenSource.ExecuteCallbackHandlers(Boolean)
  FileProviders.Physical.PhysicalFilesWatcher.RaiseChangeEvents(Object)
  System.Threading.TimerQueue.FireNextTimers()

thread-pool thread: the host starting
  System.Threading.Monitor.Enter_Slowpath(Object)                       <- waits for _callbackLock
  Primitives.CompositeChangeToken.OnChange(Object)
  Primitives.CompositeChangeToken.get_HasChanged()
  Kestrel.Core.Internal.CertificatePathWatcher.AddWatchUnsynchronized(CertificateConfig)
  Kestrel.Core.Internal.CertificatePathWatcher.UpdateWatches(List`1, List`1)   <- holds _metadataLock
  Kestrel.KestrelConfigurationLoader.Reload()
  Kestrel.Core.KestrelServerImpl+<BindAsync>d__31.MoveNext()
  Kestrel.Core.KestrelServerImpl+<StartAsync>d__28`1.MoveNext()

```

(`ChangeToken.OnChange` and `RegisterChangeTokenCallback` are inlined between `get_HasChanged` and `AddWatchUnsynchronized`.)

10.0.402 (SDK); runtime 10.0.13

- ASP.NET Core version: 10.0.13 (Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 10.0.13, host commit 4099f83977)

Issues.Title: The non-scaffolded razor page "Register" does not recognise Password.RequiredLength.
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug
Setting password length through 
```
public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services){
  ...
  services.Configure<IdentityOptions>(options =>
  {
    options.Password.RequiredLength = 1;
  });
  ...
```
does not change the non-scaffolded razor page as it always says "The Password must be at least 6 and at max 100 characters long." if inputed password is < 6 characters.

### To Reproduce

2. Select "Web application (Model-View Controller)" 
3. Select "Change authentication"
3.1. Select "Individual User Account"
4. Select Ok to have the project scaffolded.
5. Open file Startup.cs
6. Add 
```
services.Configure<IdentityOptions>(options =>
{
  options.Password.RequiredLength = 1;
});
```
to method `ConfigureServices`.
7. Press F5 (or select your favourite start-debug method).
8. In the web browser that pops up
8.1. Select Register
8.2. Type "a@example.com" as user name (or select your favourite fast-to-type email addresss).
8.3. Type "a" as password (or any password shorter than 6 characters).
8.4. Select Register

### Expected behavior
The web page should have been updated with information about successful creation of user.

### Actual behaviour
The web page says "The Password must be at least 6 and at max 100 characters long."

### Additional context
I have a question at stack overflow https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53620708/how-do-i-set-password-options-in-aspnet-core-2-1 that explains the same issue if this is not clear enough.

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

Issues.Body:
My security team escalated to me that the `PasswordHasher` is vulnerable to heap inspection, as the password is of type `String`. 
It should be instead a byte array / span of bytes cleared at the end of the process, as it is done by any cryptographic operation in corefx. CC @bartonjs.
Same problem with any password related types (`IPasswordValidator`, and maybe also the `IUserPasswordStore`)

Issues.Title: Feedback: ensure that .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling only supported in VS 2017 and won't be supported in VS 2019
Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "[Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time" (#537)

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

If you were not calling `app.UseAntiforgery()` before you will start using CSRF protection as the defense mechanism from now on.

### Affected APIs

None. This is a behavioral change affecting Blazor SSR form processing and antiforgery-token generation.

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

> Update: The ASP.NET Core 2.3 end of support date was updated from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages (latest patched version only) are currently [supported](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/aspnet#dotnet-core) on .NET Framework, following the support cycle for those .NET Framework versions. After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

## Impact of end of support

After ASP.NET Core 2.3 reaches end of support:

- No new security updates will be issued for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- Continuing to use an unsupported version may expose your applications to security vulnerabilities.
- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- The ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages will be deprecated.

## Upgrade recommendation

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

To help with the upgrade process, we recommend using [GitHub Copilot modernization](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/porting/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview), which provides AI-powered assistance to help you analyze, plan, and execute your migration to a modern .NET version.

Issues.Title: Add automation to create docs tracking issues for breaking changes
Issues.Body:
Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

## Implementation

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

- Triggers on `issues.opened` and `issues.labeled` events with "Breaking change" label
- Creates issue in docs repo with:
  - Title: `[Breaking Change] <original title>`
  - Body: Link to source issue, full context
  - Labels: `breaking-change`, `aspnet/Announcements`
- Posts comment on source issue with link to docs issue

## Duplicate Prevention

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating
- Concurrency control keyed on issue number

## Error Handling

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

## Setup Required

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`
